speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Just before the house adjourned on Tuesday last, Mr. Speaker, I moved the following amendment:
We respectfully regret that Your Excellency's present advisers have not taken such steps as are necessary to deal adequately with unemployment, to reduce the burden imposed by the public debt, and' to put the agricultural industry on a basis that will insure to the farmer a decent standard of living.
In our judgment there are three outstanding questions confronting the people of Canada, to the solution of which the government after some three years have made no very great contribution. The first question is that of unemployment; the'second is that of the public debt-and I think I might add of private debts as well-and the third is the deplorable position of the agricultural industry. In that connection also I might add the fishing industry, which is almost as badly off.
It is not my intention to quote any elaborate statistics with regard to unemployment; in fact it is almost impossible to obtain any accurate statistics. At best those in charge of the statistical department will give us only a rough estimate. Possibly however we may have some idea of the real situation when we remember that there are under relief to-day in Canada 1,220,000 individuals, including men, women and children. Some of these, of course, are among the number being assisted in the dried out constituencies of Saskatchewan. But, even making allowance for these it is obvious that a very large number are under relief because of unemployment. In my own province of Manitoba, for example, I find that in December a total of 81,943 persons were receiving unemployment relief. This figure shows an increase of 9,434 over the total for December, 1932. Other parts of the country tell a similar story.
I do not intend to quote the pre-election promises of the Prime Minister and other members of the government, as has been done so frequently in this house, but I do want to take this occasion to plead for the unemployed. I know that a constitutional question is involved. Men on both sides of the house admit that the British North America Act does not divide general and local powers in accordance with modern developments, and when it comes to a question of unemployment it seems as though we are touching one of those questions in connection with which a revision of the British North America Act is most required. It is quite obvious that the occasional case of poverty that we had sixty years ago could be dealt with locally, and was essentially a local responsibility, but I need not urge that unemployment on the vast scale that we have to-day is in a totally different category from the few needy individuals who were under poor relief sixty years ago. If we had a famine, a plague or a flood the federal government would have no hesitation in coming to the assistance of a province. I suggest that wide-spread unemployment is almost as disastrous as a flood or a plague, and until such time as we can secure

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
an amendment to the British North America Act which will legally place all responsibility upon the shoulders of the federal government -where I believe, it ought to be-it seems to me that the federal government should be willing to assume the responsibility. As it is to-day we have a tri-partite arrangement under which the federal government gives a certain proportion of relief, the provincial another, and the municipal another. As the years have gone on the provinces-this applies at least to those in the west-have become less and less able to assume their share of this burden, and the municipalities are in a worse plight. Several of the schemes that we have are dependent on the cooperation of the municipality, but in many instances those municipalities are not in a position to put up the necessary funds.
Just before I left home I met a delegation from a small municipality in my own district where certain individuals wanted to be sent out under the farm scheme. As it was under an administrator the municipality could not possibly advance the funds necessary, hence the men who were very needy could not come under the governmental scheme. In fact, in that same municipality men told me that they were living in a condition very little removed from serfdom, that they could not leave the municipality even for a few days without reporting to the relief officer. If they failed to comply with such regulation they were immediately cut off from relief. That is not a condition which should prevail in a free country.
Then, as to food, many families are receiving an amount smaller than that which is necessary to maintain them in proper health. I wonder whether we realize, too, that very often the clothing is altogether inadequate. The difficulty is that it is not merely insufficient to keep out the cold in this extreme winter weather, but in addition to that it is contributed very largely by private and philanthropic relief agencies of various kinds, with the result that for some years a great many people have been forced to be clothed with second-hand clothing. I believe that has a most demoralizing influence on a family. I suggest that very few of us could stand up under that kind of thing month after month and year after year.
Then, there is the question of shelter. I believe it is generally recognized that in order to maintain an ordinary family in decency there should be so many rooms in which they are to live. Many families are being huddled into a single room,-men, women and children

indiscriminately. Social workers are meeting with cases of immorality with which they have to deal, and which have arisen through such housing conditions.
Another difficulty which comes before u* very frequently in this extremely cold weather is that concerning fuel. Food, clothing and shelter used to be considered sufficient to cover all the vital needs, but in these days we need fuel. In many parts of the country, particularly in the west, there is no wood available. Frequently coal is not supplied, and often when there is a supply of wood it is of a very poor type, such as poplar which will not burn throughout an entire night, a condition which is not pleasant in our forty-below-zero weather, and one which causes great suffering to women and children. Such matters are not taken into consideration when relief measures are considered.

One hon. member from Montreal has suggested that Mr. Holt is cutting off the light. There is not much

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
doubt but that is the case in Montreal. Then, there is the difficulty I mentioned the other day, namely that of medical attendance. Hardly any family can get through a year without some medical or dental attendance. So far our relief arrangements have made no provision for such attendance. While sometimes people can get through a few months without medical attendance, as year after year goes by teeth will decay, adenoids and all that *sort of thing witl develop. In some cases glasses have to be obtained, if children are to have the benefit of education. These contingencies are not fully provided for.
In addition to that, though some may think that I am now going too far afield, I would point out that a great many children cannot even get the money to buy the necessary school books, pencils, scribblers-those little things that may be thought beneath the dignity of parliament to consider but which are very vital indeed when you come to the family budget.
There is the question of recreation. We cannot hope that whole families will go along year after year without any provision for recreation. At least the families will not be in very good condition if they do so. This opens up a tremendous field. I think of the fathers, many of them going along from year to year without any employment and losing their self-respect. I think of the mothers becoming discouraged, unable to maintain their hope for the future. I think of the children growing up never having known their father to be at work, never having known what it is for the family to be independent, and they themselves without any prospect even of securing a job.

That is quite true, but they are comparatively rare. My point is that even the best families are going to suffer deterioration under conditions that now prevail.
Then there is the question of the single men, of whom more than 48,000 are to-day employed chiefly in our relief camps. These relief camps are being maintained under the Department of National Defence. I do not think it is a good thing that this relief work should be placed under the military in any way whatever. I admit that these men are receiving decent food, and in many cases clothing and shelter, but I do submit that there is nothing in the life of the relief camp to give these men any real hope. I think it is the surest way to develop bums and criminals.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

offence.

Yes it is, and it should be so considered, and ruled out of order. But in all seriousness I do suggest that you cannot expect young men in the prime of life to go into these camps to get a bare living month after month, and some of them year after year, without their losing hope.-I think of the moral influences which prevail in such places. Young men who under normal circumstances would have a certain amount of social life and would look forward to marrying and rearing their own families are now deprived of all the amenities of home life and are simply kept in these camps for an indefinite future. Really I wonder that there are not more criminal acts in this country than there have been in the immediate past.
I also think of some of the younger people in their parents' homes some of whom have passed out of school but cannot get work, and some of whom have never yet had a job. I know some children who are repeating their last year in school simply because there is nothing else for them to do. Others of them are wandering around the streets and contracting all sorts of bad habits.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that this is a serious national situation that confronts us, and I submit that if this kind of thing is allowed to continue very much longer it will be impossible to maintain the morale of our people.
Further, there has been an enormously heavy expenditure with nothing to show for it. A few years ago the Prime Minister stated that he was opposed to the dole, and he provided a measure of public works. Later on it was said that the public works were too expensive, and we went back again to the dole.

We are being required to pay an ever-increasing amount of fixed charges while we are receiving smaller and smaller amounts with which to carry that burden. Surely this kind of thing must inevitably lead to disaster.
I come now to the second question, that of the public debt. Every year we have presented to this house large blocks of expenditures which are classed as uncontrollable expenditures. These are increasing steadily from year to year. We sometimes make a cut in the services to the public but we never think of cutting the interest charges. I do not think this matter has ever been better put than it was by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in the statement he made before the committee on monetary and financial

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
questions at the Imperial economic conference of 1932. I should like to quote one or two paragraphs, as follows:
Interest charges represent the most important of the fixed or semi-rigid elements in our cost structure. If prices remain on their present level, such charges will constitute an intolerable or almost intolerable burden in many cases. Even if it can be borne, the fortuitous gain to the creditor of 40 to 48 per cent in general purchasing power above what he contracted for appears to be a grave injustice.
That is the contention we have been making for a great many years in this corner of the house; the bondholder is receiving almost half as much more than the amount to which he is entitled. The Prime Minister admits that he is not entitled to receive what, to use his own words, is a fortunate gain. But we the taxpayers of the country are continuing to pay it. I ask the Prime Minister: What is he doing about that situation? His government has been carrying on for over three years now, and there has been no effort whatever to reduce that burden of public debt.

Let me pass on now to the other matter which we have included in our resolution, that is, the deplorable condition of agriculture. We cannot hope for general prosperity in this country unless there is an improvement in agricultural conditions. It becomes necessary to bring the prices of agricultural and other primary products somewhat into line with those of other commodities. I know that this is a problem that faces all countries, but none the less it is a matter of concern to Canada. Here again I think perhaps I am on safe ground if I quote from the Prime Minister himself. In the same statement from which I quoted a few minutes ago, before the committee on monetary and financial questions of the Imperial economic conference of 1932 he said:
Canada, like all other countries, has suffered severely from the calamitous fall in commodity prices. Since August, 1929, our index of wholesale prices has fallen 32 per cent and' is now only 4 per cent above the pre-war level. This means that the dollar has increased in purchasing power by 48 per cent. As a result of this rapid and persistent decline in the general price level and the inevitable disparities created between different kinds of prices, normal business relationships have been disrupted, profit margins have disappeared in many cases, enterprise has been discouraged, unemployment has steadily increased, the fiscal problems of all our public bodies have been greatly aggravated, and' the burden of fixed charges is exerting an almost intolerable pressure upon some of the strategic elements in our national economy.
Only a few facts need be cited to illustrate the way in which the traditional alignment of economic forces in this country have been sundered by the different rates of speed at which the various parts of our price structure have succumbed to the deflationary pressure of falling prices.
While wholesale prices have been falling 35 per cent, our cost of living index number has fallen only 19 per cent. On this basis the purchasing power of the dollar has increased 24 per cent.
Prices for raw materials, here as elsewhere, have fallen much more rapidly than wholesale prices generally. Thus, prices of raw and partly manufactured materials have fallen 47-3 per cent since August, 1929, whereas prices of fully and chiefly manufactured' articles have declined only 26-0 per cent. Farm products have been particularly hard hit, the decline averaging 56-4 per cent. Wheat, the staple of the western farmer, has fallen from an average price of $1.50 per bushel in 1926 to 55 cents in June, 1932, a drop of 63-3 per cent, giving an index of 36-7 as compared with one of 70 for manufactured goods at wholesale.

There again we come to the British North America Act. I submit that if this federal government were serious about the matter it would be comparatively easy to arrange such matters at least with the three prairie provinces, that are most concerned. We have the fruit-growers of British Columbia begging for some sort of legislation to be enacted here in order that they may be able to control their product in British Columbia. I think the time has about come that the public will not much Longer tolerate this shoving of the matter by the federal government over to the provinces and the provinces footballing it back to the federal government. Where there is a will there is a wayl
Only the other day in Manitoba I was handed a memorandum by an actual working farmer which I think fairly well puts the

position as the farmers, or at least a considerable number of them in the west, see the situation. I should like to read a few paragraphs :
First let me ask: Does the farmer as the primary producer of food, perform a necessary service to society in general that entitles him to a decent living, an opportunity to retire at sixty or seventy years of age on something better than our present old age pension, and in the meantime be able to pay his way, pay taxes and have some slight chance to keep free from the nightmare of debt that is his present heritage? If the answer is yes, then why do the people in the urban centres of this dominion "through the medium of the processors and distributors of foodstuffs" absolutely refuse to pay to the farmer the costs of production of the food they eat? . . .
I think it is clear that the farmer to-day is producing at less than cost price, and at less than a price that would enable him to maintain a decent Standard of living. It may be that ia very large proportion of the difference between the cost price and the sale price, is taken by middlemen, but in that case the government must intervene. He goes on:
The railways charge the same or higher rates on all our products. The commissions for selling grain and live stock and charges at stockyards are the same as when prices were three times what they are now. Packers and retailers are charging for their services, a higher percentage of the retail selling price than ever before, with the inevitable result that the portion of the consumer's dollar that now reaches the farmer is the lowest in the history of this dominion, and as a result our purchasing power has almost vanished. . . .
I wish the eastern manufacturers could really see the significance of the failure of the western farmers. I cannot see how the east is going to be prosperous unless we have prosperity among our farmers in the west and our farmers all over. I continue to read:
No appreciable or permanent improvement will or can ever take place until some system is devised whereby the price levels of the main necessities of life are permanently fixed and stabilized in as far as that portion of farm produce that is consumed in Canada is concerned', and some definite control established over processors, distributors, etc., so that each may receive their fair and just share of the final retail price according to the service they perform.
My farmer friend then goes into some computations as to what has been lost in the last two or three years by the farmers of the three prairie provinces; that is, taking the price level of 1929 and comparing it with the price levels of later years and showing the smaller returns that go to the farmer. Then with regard to grain, suppose a dollar a bushel represents a fair return to the farmer for his wheat; the difference between this and

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
the price he has actually been receiving means an enormous loss to the farmer. It is a mere guess, but it is calculated that through changes in the price level the farmers of western Canada have tost in the last three years something like half a billion dollars. Let me point out that if that figure is at all correct that means half a billion dollars less of spending power, and that affects the whole country.
My farmer friend goes on to offer a suggested resolution which I think is worthy of consideration by this house; I offer the first part of it:
In view of the fact that agriculture is in a most deplorable condition, having suffered more than any other industry from the depression, loss of markets and the foreign exchange situation. and that there is no improvement in world markets yet in sight;
This house hereby instructs the government to at once to appoint a non-partisan board or boards with full and arbitrary powers to, first, determine and fix a fair price that shall be paid to all primary producers of the main necessities of life, food, clothing and fuel that are produced and consumed in Canada, and control the marketing of same; second, determine and fix maximum prices that may be charged by those engaged in transporting, processing and distributing said necessities within the confines of this dominion; third, to have complete control of the marketing abroad of all surpluses of agricultural products that may be under price control.
When the government is so solicitous of the welfare of big industries in this country, so careful to protect them from outside competition. so careful to see to it that there are such arrangements as will enable the banks to maintain their earnings and to enable the railways, if not to maintain their earnings at least to guarantee their shareholders from loss, it does seem to me that the time has come when something should be done for the agricultural worker in this country.

As we look over the situation in Canada and in the world, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that our problems are too serious for us to spend very much time in this kind of party bickering. I believe that the time has come when the people of Canada are expecting some action to be taken. We have not confidence in this present government, as is indicated by our vote the other night and by our own amendment. But at the same time, if the present government would give us a lead in the way of a solution of the problems I have indicated, I think it would receive the full support of members in this corner of the house. We are far more concerned with the condition of the people in this country than we are with the party game. Many of us come directly from the people and are living close to them and we realize the seriousness of the situation. There is hardly anyone who does not recognize that democracy is on trial to-day. People outside are saying, what good is parliament; what is parliament for if it cannot solve these big problems of unemploy' ment, a demoralized agricultural industry, and the intolerable burden of debts?
We have been departing very largely in recent years from our older Canadian ideals. In the earlier days we believed that everyone should have a chance. I do not believe that it can honestly be said by any member here to-day that in these days every Canadian has a chance. I think of all these young people who are growing up in our homes; they have not the chance that their fathers had; they have not even the chance that their grandfathers had, because if their grandfathers worked hard enough and slaved long enough hours they had a chance to make a decent living. But our people under modern conditions have not even a chance to work. So I say we are departing from the old Canadian ideal that everyone should have a chance.
In the old days when our forefathers settled here all men were more or less equal. One might have fifty acres, another a hundred, and another two hundred, but substantially we weire all more or less on an equality and were good neighbours. To-day that is all changed. We have, on the one hand, great aggregations of wealth, and on the other hand, unemployment and insecurity. I believe the time has come when we shall have to get back to the older Canadian ideals and provide for a greater measure of equality among the

people. I do not see how Canada can be maintained as a democracy unless we have in very large measure economic equality.
With regard to democracy itself, it may be that we still have the forms of democracy, but I submit that as long as the big moneyed interests have so much influence in the formulation and control of the policies of this country we cannot be said to have any real democracy. As I pointed out the other day, in Newfoundland they have surrendered even the forms of democracy, and that former independent dominion is now being administered by a board responsible to London. The western provinces of this country were almost threatened by our Prime Minister a year ago, in a letter he wrote, that unless they could balance their budgets, or more nearly so, it might be that he would require them to appoint an administrator 'acceptable to this government who would carry on the affairs of the province. Where is our democracy going under those circumstances? Already many municipalities are in that very position. So I say that although we have the forms, we are losing the real sense and the real benefits of democracy. It would seem that at the beginning of a new session of this parliament we should once and for all forget our party squabbling and get down to real business.
I submit that we have a right under the present circumstances to demand that if the government is to remain the government of this country, it must make a determined effort to solve some of these outstanding problems that confront the people of Canada to-day.

I had the honour to be chairman of that committee, and we went into the matter with very great care. At the commencement of the labours of that committee, we received
numerous telegrams, all originating from one source, protesting against the abolition of the . tribunals. This was taken to mean by many that they did not care to have the personnel dropped, and during the first three days of our debates in the committee it became increasingly apparent that in order to satisfy some of the members at least, an arrangement should be made.
The bill that we were examining was Bill No. 78, for the purpose of shortening the procedure in soldiers' claims, so that finality would be had within a shorter time. I pointed out to the committee that I did not believe that any government or the minister would accept a proposition of that kind. I spoke to members of the legion, to Major Roper, the head of the legion, on this matter, and pointed out to him that as it was very necessary in the interests of the soldier that the legislation should pass we might come to some other arrangement. Subsequently Major Roper and I prepared a resolution which passed the committee. This resolution was for the purpose of dissolving the old Board of Pension Commissioners and also the tribunals and forming a new board to be known as the Canadian pension commission. Nothing was suggested in any way or shape as to who should be the members of this commission. The only point that was raised was as to who should be eligible, and it was mutually agreed that the members of the then tribunals should be eligible for appointment to this commission. We had no power to go further had we chosen to do so.
I might also point out that in the latter days of that committee several other resolutions were brought forward which we were unable to deal with but which we passed, and instead of incorporating them in the ordinary report I had them forwarded to the Prime Minister for his attention. Had there been an arrangement such as stated by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre it could have properly been brought forward in some such resolution. I have no desire, sir, to indulge in any partisan criticisms of the government in their administration of the affairs of this country for the last three and a half years. I appreciate the difficulties with which the members of the administration have to cope. Their every day routine duties in the ordinary course of events added to the problems which have come to the government during the present depression occupy their minds and activities but this does not excuse the administration from trying to grapple definitely with the vital causes of tihe present depression and from enunciating and putting into action policies which might be expected to improve conditions.
I am not going to indulge in recriminations but I think it should be remembered that the present government, and more particularly the leader of the government (Mr. Bennett), asked for the responsibilities with which the people of Canada have entrusted them. I do not intend to dwell upon the promises made by the Prime Minister other than to say that with the intelligence which he possesses to such a high degree he must have known that those promises could not be fulfilled. The people of Canada are entitled to some definite action in the long crisis in which the country finds itself. I regard the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) as my personal friend and he has stated in his own picturesque language that the house is on fire and that it is our duty to attend to the putting out of the conflagration. May I say to him that the house has been burning for almost four years and I think the people of Canada have nearly reached the conclusion that since the present administration has not had any great success in subduing the fire, it is about time we changed the fire brigade.
During the course of his remarks the other day the Prime Minister referred to the fact that each morning on his way to his office he passed the statue of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He made certain remarks in connection with that but I would say to him in all sincerity that when he enters this building each day he should read and reflect upon the inscription over the doors of this building which reads, "Where there is no vision, the people perish." If I have any outstanding criticism to make of the government it is this: I gathered from the remarks of the Prime Minister the other 
day in Toronto that he is convinced not only that Canada is sound-I believe that-but that conditions are basically sound and it is not necessary for him to take any particularly drastic steps to bring about what I consider to be necessary to correct present conditions m Canada. I think he is on record as saying when he left the boat at Montreal some time ago upon returning from England that he was opposed to higher wages.

The other day in Toronto he made the statement that the government had nothing spectacular to offer. I have no particular fault to find with that statement, but he went on to say that all he could suggest was hard work and thrift. Such a statement might be all right to people who have employment and who are receiving something in the way of wages with which they can exercise the virtue of thrift, but it is this statement that causes me to rise to-day. It seems to me that the statement that hard work and thrift are the only remedies for the Canadian people shows a mental attitude on the part of the Prime Minister that nothing is to be done, that he is going to stand pat and that we are not to have any definite policies to correct the conditions under which we labour to-day. He seems to think that everything is basically sound, our financial system, our industrial system and all the rest of it. He seems to think that if we only wait and work hard and apply thrift, everything will be as we should like it to be. With that statement I take absolutely definite issue. I do not see how any intelligent man who has observed the trend of circumstances in this country during the last few years and who has seen the tremendous changes which have taken place during the last ten, fifteen or twenty years in industrial relations and the crowding of people into factories in our cities, can help but realize that something is wrong. These conditions should be studied very carefully and a conscientious government should try at least to apply some remedies.
It is a definite law of nature, in the animal world, the vegetable world and the human world, that when great changes take place it is absolutely necessary that those who may be affected by such changes should adapt themselves to the new conditions. If they do not, the penalty is that they must perish. It would be unfortunate if we passed out of this depression-perhaps not to the heights of the so-called prosperity which we had in 1928 and 1929-and made no changes in our manner of meeting conditions which will recur again and again. I say with absolute conviction that when they do recur, they will be
worse than they have been during the present depression. I believe that many of the capitalists-may I call them that?-or the leading men of this country realize this fact to-day and many of them are quite ready to follow this or any other government that will institute some real remedy to provide a correction of the difficulties under which we labour. The statement has been made that this depression is world-wide. That may be perfectly true but it does not follow that we in Canada cannot do something to set our own house in order.
I do not propose to traverse the whole field of whatever remedies might be suggested; instead, I will confine myself particularly to one or two. And the leader of the C.C.F. has already touched very largely on 1 some of the question which I should like to discuss. If we are to find a remedy we must know the causes of the condition that is to be remedied. Of course, the real basic and fundamental cause is the selfishness of the human heart; there is no doubt about that. Every man looks out for himself, and it is perhaps not to be wondered at, when people have no certainty as to what is going to happen in the future to themselves and to those who depend upon them, that every man tries to secure for himself all that is possible. Perhaps it was with a realization of that fact that the Prime Minister-and I say this with all respect to him-made the statement about two years ago that nothing but the grace of God could save Canada.
I intended to speak of unemployment and the question of the debt, as well as of the Canadian National Railways, and then finally if I have time,-because it is the most important subject before us now-to discuss what can be done so that there shall not be, to put it bluntly, so great a spread between the wages of capital and the wages of labour, so that the man who works, the man who produces, may receive something that is more a just approximation to what he deserves than he has received in the past, which I believe is the cause, generally speaking, of the difficulty that faces us to-day. The remedies involve a change from selfishness to unselfishness, the realization if you like of the dependence of one on another, and the recognition of the great fact of the brotherhood of man.

There is no doubt in my mind that eventually, and probably very soon, there will have to be some control over these large corporations which to-day find themselves without control of themselves. When you talk of rugged individualism I often think of the workingman arriving at the shop in the morning, being told to hang his hat upon a certain peg, take his place at a certain machine, go through certain operations at a given rate of speed at a certain time of the day, and then return home with his day's work done. Whether he is able to carry on or not at the required rate of speed in our modern industrial plants depends entirely on his physique.
Sometimes I also wonder if the man who clips coupons from the bonds that made such a plant possible, a plant that he has possibly never seen, and the products of which are turned out by men that he has probably never seen and certainly does not know-I wonder whether that requires of the bondholder a
very great deal of rugged individualism. So far as those who are at the very head of these large industries are concerned, the executives, those who control, to-day and for some years past their individualism depends entirely on their ability to produce dividends. If they cannot do that, they are moved out and someone else takes their place. But that is not the case where there is ownership management, and that is something that will have to be taken into consideration in connection with these large concerns and be corrected.
It is also just as well-known on this side of the house as on the other side or in the corner, that people in industry to-day are not receiving the wages that they should receive to live properly. They are probably receiving all the wages that industry can give and continue to exist, but it is not sufficient to enable the workmen to live properly and carry out those duties and rights that an individual has in this country.
There is another thing that must be faced, and faced soon, by organized society because it is now very evident in every industrial centre, and that is that at the age of forty-five a man to-day is thrown upon the street.
I know whereof I speak. In the shops in my own city to-day a man of forty-five years of age has no chance of securing a position, and when a man of that age is in a position, ways and means are found of seeing that he is let out certainly by the time he reaches fifty. These things react upon society because men who have worked a great length of time at one job are not fit for anything else, and when they are thrown out of work they are unable to take care of themselves; for I defy any man to say that at present wages a man can work from the age of twenty to forty-five years and in that time acquire sufficient _ to take care of himself for the rest of his life. It cannot be done, and that is something which the state, which after all is organized society, will have to take into consideration, and undoubtedly the sooner it is done the better.
I could go on and mention a number of other things that even the return of prosperity as we know it will not right. It is said and believed by everyone here I think that we have reached the ceiling of production in agriculture. We are producing more agricultural products than can be consumed. We are not producing anything like what the land in cultivation and the machinery available will produce. A short time ago I read a statement made in a report, I think of an agriculture committee in the United States, to the effect that fifteen per cent or less of

The Address-Mr. Morand

the people of any nation could, if properly organized, produce all the food necessary for the rest of the nation. With these things kept in view there is no doubt that there must be some lopping off and some changes made in the control. But even though these things are facing us 1 do not think it is necessary to scrap the entire system and to forget all that has been developed down through the ages. We should not throw over all those things which the people stand for and which are based mostly upon natural rights and natural laws. We should not adopt a new system of government such as we hear explained in this house in such a flimsy and cloudy manner. We should not adopt a type of government which cannot effectively be put into operation.
It is said that this government has been a government of laissez-faire, that there has been nothing done. When I hear statements such as the one just made by my hon. friend across the way, that any improvement is due to the policies of Mr. Roosevelt, I sometimes wonder if real attention has been paid to what has been done during the last three years. Surely the changes which have occurred in Oreat Britain have not been due to Mr. Roosevelt. Surely some credit should be given to this government for the additional markets which were opened up through the imperial economic conference. Surely the higher prices received by the farmers of this country as compared with those received by the farmers in the United States is not due to the policies of Mr. Roosevelt. The farmers of Canada are receiving higher prices for their products than the farmers of the United States where Mr. Roosevelt's policies are being applied. This government had the courage to meet the situation. I am proud to be sitting behind my leader; I am glad to be supporting a government which had the courage to put on such tariffs as were necessary at a time when the whole edifice of this country would have been ruined with the dumping of commodities from other countries. Despite the cry of importers, despite the cry of those who would have gained for the time being through the importation of cheap articles into this country at the cost of our own industries and the exportation of our capital, they saw fit to put on a tariff of sufficient height to provide work within our own country.

speechtext: Yes, it has been done by the municipalities, but let me tell my hon. friend of what has occurred in my own municipality. maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean to say that the giving of relief strikes at the causes of the depression? Is it not merely helping out, the duty of any humanitarian government? It does not strike at the root of the trouble.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: There is no question but that it was the duty of the government, but they had the courage to face that duty.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext: You had the support of the whole house in that.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
We did not always have the support of the whole house. Your right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) was not always as quick to give that support.
We find that during the eight years that hon. friends opposite were in power and when there was great credit expansion, no control was exercised. This government has had the courage to bring before the house legislation to create a central bank, which will undoubtedly exercise such control as will prevent the large inflations and deflations of credit which have occurred. We find also that the construction of public works is being revived in an attempt to give work to as many as possible. Many of the provinces started such

The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Teace River)
a program but found it was too expensive. It was found that the carrying out of public works and the spending of money did not increase the purchasing power of the country as it should. The matter was allowed to drift, but the government now feels that it is justified in starting a building program in an effort to get as many of our people back to work as possible. We must not forget that the mere spending of money does not increase the purchasing power of the people. For the last three years I have heard my hon. friends in the corner claim that the spending of money on public works would increase purchasing power. So long as the financial institutions of this country continue to call in their credits, all that this would amount to is that the money paid out would be used in the paying of debts and the wiping out of credits. You might spend fifty, seventy-five or a hundred million dollars and not increase the purchasing power by one cent. When the reduction of credit has reached a point where it can go no further, the money spent is distributed throughout the country and the purchasing power is increased.
I should like to suggest to the government that in the carrying out of this program consideration should be given to the possibility of diverting a certain amount of this money in order to buy up stock and provide for loans or bonuses to new industries, industries that are indigenous to the country, industries that will fill a void which we are now having to supply from outside. Perhaps I might give an example; I suggest the sugar beet industry. We import 85 per cent of the sugar we use in this country, and we have land that is capable of growing sugar beets, besides farmers who need that source of employment. We have a market in our own country and the difficulty is to finance such an institution. I would respectfully submit to the government therefore that they think seriously of devoting a certain proportion of that money to the financing of such an industry. It is different from public works. Once an amount of money has been spent to provide employment in the construction of public works, no further work is available; indeed, instead of providing work such a construction is only too often an expense. But when you spend a certain amount of money to assist in the financing of such an industry as I suggest, after the building program is completed there is continuous employment from year to year in the area where the building has been constructed.
I am satisfied that this government fully realizes the situation in Canada; I am satisfied that it is advancing as rapidly as it can
in the light of the knowledge it is bound to have, its members sitting as they do on this side; and I am satisfied that the people of Canada are more anxious to see a gradual but steady improvement in conditions, with a gradual change in that part of our system that may be at fault, than they are to see a new order brought about, a new order that might only turn out to be a Frankenstein which will destroy the very ideals they wish to have realized.
I have faith in Canada. I am not quite so much alarmed about the debts of the country as some others whom I hear around me. Let us not forget this fact-that the debts of a country, so long as they are within the country, are the riches of the inhabitants of the country. What we owe within the country is the richness of the country. It is taxable; it is wealth, and is just as much on the credit as on the debit side. Moreover, we have not tapped the natural resources of the country, and in Canada we can create ample wealth. In this dominion, with the knowledge, the education and the science we have at our disposal, we can create all that we need, all that is necessary to make this a real country; and I am convinced that with proper administration, slowly, if you will, but surely, and profiting by the experience we have had in the last few years, not being afraid of changes -and I do not believe for one minute that this government is afraid of changes, for it has given ample evidence that it is not- Canada will come out of the depression completely, as it is coming out to-day better than any other country in the world.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am mot able to agree with every statement in the speech from the throne, I do not see in it anything to which I am opposed, any major legislative proposals to which I can object. When the bills embodying the legislation there referred to are presented to the house, differences of opinion about details may arise and we may change our view's regarding them, but with the proposals concerning agriculture, silver-I am not sure that I know much about silver-a central bank, the wheat agreement, the agricultural credit question and assistance to the provinces, in principle I am in hearty accord. That is the reason I voted as I did the other day on the straight want of confidence motion, a motion that was purely negative and con-
618	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
tained no constructive proposal. For years I have taken the stand in my constituency that I would not support such a motion except when a vote of want of confidence was practically the only way to deal with the question at issue, and especially not when there was before us a definite proposal in the way of a program of legislation.
However, while I agree with these proposals, I do not think they go far enough. I have at times voted on various proposals affecting unemployment, agriculture and debt that I think require attention, and for that reason I intend to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). We have heard a great deal in the last four years about depression, and how Canada is pulling through. We have' heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) say the banks were-what was it, the sheet anchor of the country? But my impression is that it is the farmers who have been the sheet anchor of the country. I am not saying that I know a great deal about the industrial centres of eastern Canada, but I submit that what has been going on on the farms of the west during the past four years is practically the conscription of the life savings of the farm population of my section of Canada, and that has largely helped Canada to weather the depression as well as she has. It may be a fine thing for an industry or institution to be able to declare dividends under the present circumstances-I do not think it is; there may be a difference of opinion about that-but the people who have been willing to put in ten hours a day working on the land or elsewhere and who have been selling their produce for about half the cost of production and even lowering their standard of living-these are the people who in my opinion have made the major contribution towards enabling Canada to weather the storm of the depression. I do not believe that this lowering of the standard of living is a good thing in itself, but they had to do it; only in this way have they been able to meet the prevailing conditions.
While I agree that there may be difficulties with regard to finance and credits, insurance companies, banks and railways, I do not believe there will be any greater difficulty in adjusting these matters than there has been in the adjustment of the agricultural and farming people to the very trying situation of the last four years.
Unemployment has been pretty well discussed: I will not touch it except to say as to public works, that so long as we do not have to go outside of Canada to obtain material or tools for the purpose, and the works are

necessary, I cannot see that we shall impoverish the country by proceeding with them, and we ought to be able to make the necessary financial adjustment to do so.
A great deal has been said as to the public debt and the debt of the national railways, and whether it was increased or decreased during certain years. It is possible, I think, to make a showing as to reduction of debt in various ways, but what we have to deal with in Canada is not merely the railway debt, not merely the debt of the dominion, the provinces or the municipalities, but all debts, including private debts. Under present conditions, where the ordinary industrious farmer in Canada cannot pay his debts or in most cases even his interest, there is need for a tremendous readjustment of price levels.
There is a reference in the speech from the throne to the improvement of prices in Canada, and the suggestion is that it is due to the wheat agreement. I think the improvement in wheat prices in Canada has been due not to a rise in wheat values in the world market so much as to a lowering of the value of money on the North American continent. Other factors may have entered into it, but in my judgment that is the chief one. I believe that by stabilization of a reasonable volume of money in circulation, and by putting hack into circulation some of that $900,000,000 that our banks have taken out of circulation in the last four years, we will find means of improving price levels within the Dominion of Canada and so making it possible to come nearer to balancing our budgets and paying our debts with reasonable interest charges thereon.
I am in favour of inflation. I do not believe the statements that have been made in this house against inflation are worth the breath they took to utter. But I do not mean that I am in favour of uncontrolled inflation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), speaking of inflation a few days ago, referred to Europe. There is no question that inflation in Europe, Germany and Austria, for example, was uncontrolled; money was inflated a hundred thousand times. I think I gave figures last year to show that if we in Canada inflated to the extent they did in Germany a bushel of wheat would be worth something like $700. Great Britain went off the gold standard. She did not go off; she was bucked off. Coming east for this session I remember reading a story about a famous horse called Midnight and the last bucking contest in which it took part. This horse never had been ridden, and the best cowboy

The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
they were able to get in a certain part of the United States was thrown in two seconds, though he was supposed to stay on the horse for eight seconds. Great Britain tried very hard to stay on the gold standard. A national government was organized; an election was held, after which the national government held a large majority in the House of Commons. This was all done to keep Great Britain on the gold standard, but within a very short time she was off the gold standard because she could not stay on it. Instead of that being a bad thing for the world, in my judgment it was a good thing; it was the first big step towards reflation, reasonable inflation, and the rise of world price levels. When the United States, under President Roosevelt, undertook to follow that lead in a more vigorous way than Great Britain has undertaken so far, it was another big step towards rescuing the world from a large measure of debt and depression. I think if the government has made one mistake in the last two or three years that is more to be regretted than any other it was the determination to hang on to what was called sound money, to O.K. deflation and refuse to follow Great Britain's lead and1 go off the gold standard in order to allow a reasonable depreciation or devalutaion of the money in the Dominion of Canada. As we increase the supply of money we decrease its value, just as we do in connection with other things.
I intend, Mr. Speaker, to vote for the amendment, and I also intend to vote for the speech from the throne. According to the rules of the house, that have been drawn up for two parties, that may be quite inconsistent. It may be inconsistent to vote no confidence in -the government and then to vote for a measure containing a number of proposals practically all of which I favour. But is that any more inconsistent than it is to vote against the address and then turn around and support the legislation after it is presented in this house? As I said the other day, in connection with these votes you are right and wrong no matter what you do. I intend to do what I think is the common sense thing to do in all the circumstances, in relation to my convictions with regard to the measures proposed.
I am not a lawyer, but I have heard a few constitutional arguments in this house; I have formed some opinions of my own, and I intend to discuss them this evening. The other day the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) went on to discuss the significance of the three recent by-elections, and he added that the government had lost the confidence
of the people because of unredeemed promises. During the course of his speech he quoted Mr. Gladstone and Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman as having expressed views which support the position he took the other night when he asked that the government should resign and go to the country. But there has been some change in constitutional practice since the days of Gladstone and Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman. What about the days of the Labour government in Great Britain? I may be wrong, but I do not recall any case when Mr. Gladstone was defeated in the house on a government measure and refused to go to the country. Under Ramsay MacDonald and the Labour party, however, we had votes of that kind time and again in the British house. I remember seeing one newspaper report that stated that the government had been defeated seven times and still did not go to the country. That was a relaxation of the previous constitutional practice.
We have also, Mr. Speaker, Canadian precedents as well as British precedents, and in connection with this very question I should like to quote what the ex-Minister of Justice said in this house. You will remember, sir, that in 1925 we had an election. If I am not mistaken the Liberals went to the country with about 117 members and came back with about 100, and when the house opened the firsit motion proposed by the then Minister of Justice was the following:
That in the opinion of this house, in view of the recent general election, the government was justified in retaining office and in summoning parliament, and the government is entitled to retain office, unless defeated by a vote of this house equivalent to a vote of want of confidence.
Then the argument began. I remember how Mr. Meighen jumped into this discussion with all his vigour. Perhaps I had better read Mr. Meighen's amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Jn the late general election the candidates of His Excellency's then advisers, at whose instance the appeal to the country was made, were defeated in a large majority of the constituencies,
That nine ministers of the crown, including the Prime Minister, were rejected at the polls and have no seats in parliament,
That the party represented in the last parliament by His Majesty's opposition secured in the said election by far the largest support in the popular vote, and has substantially the largest number of members of any party in the present House of Commons.
In discussing the matter the then Minister of Justice said:
My right hon. friend is one in parliament, as I am one. We are all equal here, and the
620	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
question whom parliament wants as the executive, the board of control, the cabinet in Canada at the present time, must be decided by members of parliament, not by the cabinet. This being the issue to decide which parliament has been summoned, after we have been charged with being usurpers who have no authority

Some hon. Members: Hear, hear.
Mr. Lapointe:	Then why does my right hon.
friend object to having that issue decided?
Mr. Wilson (Wentworth):	The people decided it.
Mr. Lapointe:	Yes, the people as represented
in parliament, not the people of one province or another. The people of all the provinces of the dominion, as represented here by the members whom they have elected, are the judges.
That is perfectly plain. The position he took was simply this, that a government that obtained a majority vote in the house had the confidence of the country. That position was different from the position taken by Gladstone and Campbell-Bannerman, but it was the sensible position to take under all the circumstances, and it is the sensible one to take now.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
This
practice of leaning on Mr. Gladstone who died years ago and on Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, rather than accepting general principles

and applying our own common sense to the situation, is a position I cannot take, and I do not intend to be snared by any such argument, regardless of who advances it. I was one of those who supported the position taken by Mr. Lapointe in 1925. I offer no apology for differing with him when he changes his position to-day.
Now then, "the government has lost confidence in the country because of its unredeemed promises". I have listened to the debate; I have heard the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) and I have heard the very excellent propagandist . speech of the right hon. gentleman who leads the official opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). What- have we got for a Liberal program? Very largely it is the Liberal platform of 1919 with a new date stamp on it. I am not going to say we ought to condemn the Liberal party because it did not carry into effect all the planks in its platform. I am not going to take that position at all. But I do think that some explanation ought to be made as to why, for instance, we are being told to-day that if they come back into office they will give us unemployment insurance. Everybody knows- and I think my friends will understand that I am making this statement because I believe it to be true-that we had fairly good times in Canada between the years 1924 and 1929. Any time Liberals review those years they say, and quite truthfully, that they did certain things-reduced for instance, the public debt, the national railways were prosperous. They say that they had large surpluses. Very well; why was not the country in a financial position to give effect to the promise with regard to unemployment insurance? Why do we have to wait until 1934 and run another campaign on it? At that time we had financial resources; we had the promise of the government in power to carry such a scheme into effect. I submit that question ought to be answered.
I now come to another point. Turning to the paragraph entitled Resolution on Encouragement to Agriculture contained in the booklet issued by the National Liberal Convention of 1919, I find the last clause reads as follows:
Your committee on agriculture begs to recommend that a special committee be appointed to prepare a resolution upon the banking system of Canada and the adapting of said system to satisfactory loans in connection with land and live stock and to present such resolution to your committee.
There is your intermediate and short term credit. But was effect given to that recommendation? It was not. Governments have

The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
within their power that which acts as a great determiner in connection with the balancing of income and the readjustment and equitable distribution of the national wealth, namely, taxation. I do not think we have ever had a government which has really made use of the powers of taxation with a view to redistributing or distributing properly the national income. From the same booklet I find a paragraph entitled Resolution on Financial Condition and Taxation. From that paragraph I shall take the last section, but if any hon. member wishes to hear the rest of it I shall be pleased to give it to him. It is as follows:
That increase of revenue must be sought from an equitable and effective imposition and collection of graduated taxes, on business profits and income, applicable to all incomes above reasonable exemptions.
I call the attention of hon. members to the expression "graduated taxes, on business profits and income." It has been stated that the period of largest profits in the history of Canada was between 1924 and 1929. In the paragraph I have just read we have reference to taxes on business profits and income. Consulting the Canada Year Book for the years 1919, 1922, 1925 and 1929 as to collections under customs taxes, business profits and income I find the following figures:

So, Mr. Speaker, what we are being offered to-day as a substitute for government policy is very largely what was offered in 1919. I think it will be generally agreed that although reductions were made in the customs tariff during some of those years, notably 1924 and 1926, the general level was not greatly reduced. May I ask, with all due respect, if a new government coming into office to-day would find it easier to reduce tariffs than the
government which took office in 1921 with about fifty-one Conservatives in the house and practically the whole of the remaining members pledged to lower tariffs? What about the general trend of tariffs in the world since that time? What about the restrictions- quotas, and so on-which Sir Arthur Salter said were due largely to the wrong operation of the monetary policies of the various countries of the world? We were told very definitely in the speech of the right hon. gentleman who leads the official opposition that what we have of depression in Canada is largely due to the policies of the government. Well, I do not think the right hon. gentleman himself agrees with that statement. In the speech in which he was discussing the C.C.F. resolution moved last year by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) he said this, and I think it is a good thing that that motion was moved because it at least brought this forth:
I remember, at the time the Liberal party appealed for office and was returned to office in 1921, conditions were not unlike those at the present time.
He then goes on to argue what they did when they were returned to power. He says:
And that is exactly what we did, and what happened. After we came into office we reversed in many particulars the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite. They had been raising tariffs, we immediately lowered tariffs. They had been introducing other measures which were restricting trade; we took steps to remove those restrictions, and in a short time, as hon. members know, instead of huge deficits and increased taxation and continued depression this country had for seven years in succession surpluses instead of deficits, reductions in the public debt accompanied by reductions in taxation, and a great increase in trade and employment, with consequent prosperity throughout the dominion.
"We did it"-that was the whole argument. He went on:
I might say that my right hon. friend in the last general election, in opposing the then Liberal administration, adopted very much the same course, only he went a great deal further in what he promised. We were then at the beginning of a part of the present world depression. My right hon. friend stated that it was due to the mistaken policies of the administration. He put it all down to the policies of the administration then in office, and he sought to win the support of the electors by stating that if returned to office he would alter those policies and put others into effect which would end unemployment.
What is the situation? When the Liberal party was in office, "we did it," so far as everything good was concerned, and anything that was open to criticism was put down to the world depression. I ask, what is the
622	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
difference between their attitude when in office and that of the present government? Exactly the same arguments were advanced by the present Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition against the Liberals, then in office, as are being advanced by the opposition to-day, and we are being asked to take those arguments seriously! And the same replies came from the other side of the house at that time as come from that side to-day-that the government's policies were responsible for anything good and that the world depression was to blame for anything bad.

With regard to the raising of tariffs, it is said that they were raised because of what had been done in other countries. But there was a strong presumption that the Canada first policy was being used to protect certain people rather than to meet world conditions. That was the impression in the country, that the primary reason for high tariffs was the protection of certain people. I do not know that it is going to be so easy to lower them

certainly no easier than it was in 1921; not so easy, I think.
To hon. members who ask what I want, may I say I want a reasonable inflation. Equipped with that experience, he had had three years in the seclusion of Laurier House or his farm in the Gatineau hills to study conditions during the years that have elapsed 
since this government came into power. Was it then not reasonable that people in western Canada should expect from a gentleman with those advantages, in comparison with others who had been entrusted with the administration of government for a very limited time, some practical, some definite suggestions of a constructive nature to help our country at the present time? But I challenge the right hon. gentleman or any hon. member of the house to state one specific constructive idea that he gave. He stated, as has been his custom, that he advocated wider markets, lower tariffs; but I think the majority of farmers in the west at least feel that there is no citizen in the Dominion of Canada who should keep a more absolute and stricter silence on the question of wider markets and tariffs as far as agricultural products are concerned than the right hon. gentleman himself. For nine years as Prime Minister of this country he saw market after market in country after country absolutely closed in many cases to the agricultural products of this country, markets that were free when he took office but around which tariff walls were put up that made it impossible for the agricultural products of this country to get in. Yet he came to the west and talked of wider markets, throwing out the inference that if he were in office now he would assure wider markets and lowering of tariffs. The only tariffs the right hon. gentleman could lower are the tariffs of this country, and to lower our tariffs would certainly not widen the markets for our agricultural products.
To show still further the inconsistency of the right hon. gentleman on that tour I will quote from a paper whose favourable attitude towards the Liberal party I think no person in this house will dispute. The right hon. gentleman after that tour came east. He went to the Liberal summer school at Port Hope. That he was assiduous in his attendance is stated by the Leader Post of Regina in its issue of September II, 1933. The report says:

The right hon. gentleman went through the west and gave the impression that if he were in power there would be wider markets and lowering of tariffs, yet at this meeting, where they were assembled for days with the best brains of the Liberal party in this dominion, and I believe some imported brains from outside the dominion, and with nothing else to engage their attention, they admitted, according to the report of their own paper, that there was nothing they could do to get wider markets other than what had been done and was being done by the present government.
I have taken longer than I had intended in this part of my address. I will now deal for a few minutes with the situation in respect to agriculture as we found it when taking office in 1930.
Tariffs had been raised in practically all countries of the world to protect their own agricultural industries, notaJbly in Germany, France, Italy and the United States. The surplus of bacon and butter that had been going from Denmark to Germany, France and Italy, also the surplus from New Zealand and Australia, being turned away from its accustomed market, had to flow into some market from which it was not shut out by tariff walls. The result was a greatly increased flow of agricultural products into the one free market of the world, that of the United Kingdom. That had such a depressing effect on the United Kingdom market that farmers were practically put out of business overnight and the world market was depressed out of all proportion to what had been the case previously.
In addition to that we in Canada had to face a condition that arose during the last year hon. gentlemen opposite were in office. By one action alone, the raising of the United States tariff against our cattle, about 145,000 head of cattle annually were shut out from the United States market. In 1929 Canada exported over 250,000 cattle to the United States, but their tariff was put up during the time hon. gentlemen opposite were in office to such an extent that only relatively few cattle could be shipped to that country. That great stream of cattle was turned back year after year for us to market somewhere else. Yet we hear hon. gentlemen opposite speak of wider markets.
In the east a similar condition arose in regard to a different commodity. For many years a great milk and cream trade had been growing up between the farmers of the 71726-40 j
eastern part of Ontario, the eastern townships of Quebec and the maritimes, and the United States, to such an extent that in 1927-28 the flow of milk and cream to the United States was sufficient to have produced 52,000,000 pounds of cheese. Imagine, then, the result of a tariff being placed against that milk and cream, turning back into the home market an additional 26,000,000 pounds of butter or, in terms of cheese, 52,000,000 pounds of cheese. Those were just some of the legacies from the previous administration with which we had to grapple when we came into power.
During the election campaign it was stated that if returned to power we would take steps immediately to give the Canadian market to the Canadian farmer. That has been done so far as it is possible for us to do it by tariff and other means. Now for a few moments I should like to deal with one other of our chief agricultural commodities, namely butter. When this government took office the butter situation in Canada was as follows: Millions of pounds had been shipped into Canada from the dominions of Australia and New Zealand. On top of that our milk and cream, as I said before, had been turned back from the United States so as to increase the production of our dairy products to the extent of about 26,000,000 pounds more butter or 52,000,000 pounds of cheese. The right hon, leader of the opposition has stated that if he were returned to power one of his objectives would be to put the tariff back to the point where it was when he went out of office. That would mean that at the present time the duty against New Zealand and Australian butter would be from one-half cent to one cent per pound. If that were true, making all allowance for extra freight and handling charges butter could have been shipped into this country from New Zealand in April last for a little over twelve cents per pound. It is a very simple matter to follow that back and to find what price would have been quoted for butter fat to the farmer living inland. To ascertain what the result would have been we will take one week, namely that ending April 15, 1933. The price of No. 1 butter in Montreal ranged from 30i to 31 cents per pound. For the month of April, 1933, Australian finest quality, which is comparable to Canadian butter, averaged in London 12-46 cents per pound. Allowing for one cent duty that butter could have been laid down for 13-46 cents, or a difference of 17-29 cents per pound less than the price our butter was bringing in Montreal. Applying this to the approximate production of 5,500,000 for one week represents a loss of $950,950. That is the effect of the statement made by the right hon. leader of the opposition. If his statement were put into dollars and cents instead of remaining, as it stands, a more or less theoretical statement, it would have cost the producers of Canada in the one week in April of 1933 which I have mentioned a little short of $1,000,000. That is for butter alone.

That means that his bacon would be accepted without duty* and he would be selling on exactly the same terms
as would the British farmer. The British government as a result of an extensive campaign investigated thoroughly the whole hog situation of the United Kingdom and decided they would have to take some steps, no matter how drastic, to raise the price of bacon in the United Kingdom to a point where it would be possible for an efficient farmer at least to earn a livelihood. Roughly what they had in mind was raising the price of bacon to eighty-five shillings per hundredweight, and they were dealing with bacon comparable in quality to that produced in Canada-and may I state in passing that the hundredweight is 112 pounds. That was made very clear at the time the Ottawa agreements were discussed in the house. It was known to every intelligent member that that was the intention of the British government. Believing that they would carry out their intention, the result could be only this: the price of hogs in Canada was bound to go up, and to go up at least double what it had been previously. That would have been the case had they carried out their intention of raising the price to eighty-five shillings per hundredweight of 112 pounds.
Hon. members in the house and out of the house, and particularly Liberal members in western Canada, knowing that the price was going to go up, through their speeches, did almost everything in their power either by omission or commission, to discourage the farmers from going into hog raising. As farmers, they knew that at least ten or twelve months would be required before any man beginning to raise hogs would have a product ready for the market. Knowing that, nothing has so much incensed me since I took office as to find that men should, through what must have been purely fanatical, political prejudice, stand in the way of their fellow farmers selling their oats and barley through the marketing of hogs for at least fifty cents a bushel instead of selling them, as they must do otherwise, for twenty-five or twenty-six cents a bushel.
Immediately after the Ottawa agreements were made I visited Toronto, where I had called a meeting of all the provincial ministers of agriculture and the experts from all agricultural colleges and provincial departments of agriculture so that without loss of time we could immediately make available all the information in front of us and send it out to the different parts of Canada so that the farmers could prepare to take the greatest possible advantage of the offer contained in the agreements. I would much rather be in the position I am in, having done that and having worked in season and out of season

since to improve the quality of our bacon and hogs and to encourage the farmers to obtain the right quality, than be in the position of those people who through lack of support are responsible for the farmers in Canada from the east to tihe west losing the millions of dollars that they are losing now because these people were not frank enough to bury their political prejudices and tell the farmers of the advantage that was being offered them.
To show how serious the United Kingdom has been in the matter of raising the price of their bacon, I will give some of the restrictions that they have placed on the importation of bacon from foreign countries. The first restriction that they placed on the importation of bacon from foreign countries was 15 per cent. That did not have very much effect because Denmark, Sweden and other countries that exported to the United Kingdom, realizing that such action was going to be taken, dumped all their available bacon into the United Kingdom market. That left a great load on that market which had first to be lifted before any effect of the restriction could be felt. The Danes went further. They cut away the poorer parts of their bacon so that they could get entry into the United Kingdom market of a greater quantity of their highest class product.
